# Task 1: Slate Health Check

## Introduction

```{r}
#| label: task1-setup
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
library(patchwork)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 9))

focus_genres <- c(
  "Action", "Comedy", "Drama",
  "Horror", "Animation"
)

movies <- read_csv("data/movies.csv",
                   show_col_types = FALSE)

movies_clean <- movies |>
  filter(!is.na(release_year),
         release_year <= 2016) |>
  mutate(
    budget = if_else(budget < 10000, NA_real_, 
                     as.numeric(budget)),
    revenue = if_else(revenue <= 0, NA_real_,
                      as.numeric(revenue)),
    roi = if_else(
      !is.na(budget) & !is.na(revenue),
      revenue / budget,
      NA_real_
    ),
    budget_m = budget / 1e6,
    franchise_status = factor(
      franchise_status,
      levels = c("Original", "Franchise")
    )
  )

movies_focus <- movies_clean |>
  filter(primary_genre %in% focus_genres)
```

## Data Preparation and quality

The data are from the course-provided movie dataset, based on The Movie Database [@tmdb]. Films released after 2016 are excluded. Budgets below $10,000 and zero revenues are treated as missing, and ROI is calculated as revenue divided by budget. For genre comparisons, each film is assigned to its first-listed genre.

The analysis excludes films released after 2016, treats budgets below $10,000 and zero revenue as missing, and recalculates ROI using valid financial observations. Each film is assigned to its first-listed (`primary_genre`) genre to avoid counting the same film multiple times.

```{r}
#| label: task1-data-quality

data_quality <- tibble(
  Measure = c(
    "Films in original dataset",
    "Films in analysis period",
    "Missing or invalid budgets",
    "Missing or invalid revenues",
    "Missing ROI values",
    "Films with valid budget and ROI"
  ),
  Count = c(
    nrow(movies),
    nrow(movies_clean),
    sum(is.na(movies_clean$budget)),
    sum(is.na(movies_clean$revenue)),
    sum(is.na(movies_clean$roi)),
    sum(complete.cases(
      movies_clean[, c("budget", "roi")]
    ))
  )
)

kable(data_quality, caption = "Data quality summary")
```

```{r}
#| label: task1-summary-table

financial_summary <- tibble(
  Variable = c("Production budget ($m)", "ROI (multiple)"),
  N = c(
    sum(!is.na(movies_clean$budget)),
    sum(!is.na(movies_clean$roi))
  ),
  Mean = c(
    mean(movies_clean$budget_m, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean(movies_clean$roi, na.rm = TRUE)
  ),
  Median = c(
    median(movies_clean$budget_m, na.rm = TRUE),
    median(movies_clean$roi, na.rm = TRUE)
  ),
  SD = c(
    sd(movies_clean$budget_m, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd(movies_clean$roi, na.rm = TRUE)
  ),
  Q1 = c(
    quantile(movies_clean$budget_m, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    quantile(movies_clean$roi, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)
  ),
  Q3 = c(
    quantile(movies_clean$budget_m, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    quantile(movies_clean$roi, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
) |>
  mutate(
    across(Mean:Q3, ~round(.x, 2))
  )

knitr::kable(
  financial_summary,
  caption = "Summary statistics for production budgets and ROI"
)
```

Of 4,801 films in the analysis period, 1,070 have an invalid or missing budget, 1,425 have missing revenue and 1,587 have missing ROI. Financial results therefore reflect only films with usable values. The median budget is **$24 million** and median ROI is **2.30**; medians are more informative than means because a few films have unusually large values.

## Overall Distributions

```{r}
#| label: fig-overall
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of budgets and ROI, and film composition."
#| fig-width: 7.3
#| fig-height: 2.2

p1 <- ggplot(
  movies_clean |> filter(!is.na(budget_m)),
  aes(x = budget_m)
) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 45,
    fill = "#3478A8",
    colour = "white"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_dollar(suffix = "m")
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Budget ($m)",
    y = "Number of films"
  )

p2 <- ggplot(
  movies_clean |> filter(!is.na(roi), roi > 0),
  aes(x = roi)
) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 45,
    fill = "#269C8C",
    colour = "white"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 1,
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "firebrick"
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(
    labels = scales::label_number()
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "ROI (log scale)",
    y = "Number of films"
  )

franchise_summary <- movies_clean |>
  count(franchise_status, name = "Films") |>
  mutate(
    Percentage = round(100 * Films / sum(Films), 1)
  )

p3 <- ggplot(
  franchise_summary,
  aes(x = franchise_status,
      y = Films,
      fill = franchise_status)
) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(Percentage, "%")),
    vjust = -0.5
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("Original" = "#3478A8",
               "Franchise" = "#E59B46")
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Film type",
    y = "Number of films"
  ) +
  guides(fill = "none") +
  expand_limits(y = max(franchise_summary$Films) * 1.1)

(p1 + p2 + p3) + plot_layout(ncol = 3)
```

Budgets are right-skewed, with most films concentrated at the lower end. ROI is also highly skewed, so it is displayed on a log scale; the dashed line marks revenue equal to budget (ROI = 1). **Original films make up 94.6%** of the dataset, compared with **5.4% franchises**.

## Differences Across Genres

```{r}
#| label: fig-genres
#| fig-cap: "Budgets, ROI and franchise composition across the five focus genres."
#| fig-width: 7.3
#| fig-height: 2.4
p4 <- ggplot(
  movies_focus |> filter(!is.na(budget_m)),
  aes(
    x = reorder(primary_genre, budget_m,
                FUN = median),
    y = budget_m,
    fill = primary_genre
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot(
    outlier.alpha = 0.2,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_dollar(suffix = "m")
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Primary genre",
    y = "Budget ($m)"
  )

p5 <- ggplot(
  movies_focus |> filter(!is.na(roi), roi > 0),
  aes(
    x = reorder(primary_genre, roi, FUN = median),
    y = roi,
    fill = primary_genre
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot(
    outlier.alpha = 0.2,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    x = "Primary genre",
    y = "ROI (log scale)"
  )

p6 <- ggplot(
  movies_focus,
  aes(
    x = primary_genre,
    fill = franchise_status
  )
) +
  geom_bar(
    position = "fill",
    width = 0.7
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_percent()
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Original" = "#3478A8",
      "Franchise" = "#E59B46"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Primary genre",
    y = "Share of films",
    fill = "Film type"
  )

(p4 + p5 + p6) + plot_layout(ncol = 3)
```

Animation and action generally have higher production budgets, while horror and drama tend to be lower-budget. ROI overlaps substantially across genres, suggesting that a larger budget does not guarantee a greater revenue-to-budget multiple. Franchise shares also vary by genre, although original films dominate all five groups.

## Changes over time

```{r}
#| label: fig-trends
#| fig-cap: "Median budgets, median ROI and film composition by release year, 1990–2016."
#| fig-width: 7.3
#| fig-height: 2.4
budget_trend <- movies_clean |>
  filter(release_year >= 1990) |>
  group_by(release_year) |>
  summarise(
    median_budget = median(budget_m, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_valid = sum(!is.na(budget_m)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(n_valid >= 5)

p7 <- ggplot(
  budget_trend,
  aes(x = release_year, y = median_budget)
) +
  geom_line(colour = "#3478A8", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(colour = "#3478A8", size = 1.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_dollar(suffix = "m")
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Release year",
    y = "Median budget ($m)"
  )

roi_trend <- movies_clean |>
  filter(release_year >= 1990) |>
  group_by(release_year) |>
  summarise(
    median_roi = median(roi, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_valid = sum(!is.na(roi)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(n_valid >= 5)

p8 <- ggplot(
  roi_trend,
  aes(x = release_year, y = median_roi)
) +
  geom_line(colour = "#269C8C", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(colour = "#269C8C", size = 1.5) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 1,
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "firebrick"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Release year",
    y = "Median ROI (multiple)"
  )

franchise_trend <- movies_clean |>
  filter(release_year >= 1990) |>
  count(release_year, franchise_status) |>
  group_by(release_year) |>
  mutate(
    percentage = n / sum(n)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

p9 <- ggplot(
  franchise_trend,
  aes(
    x = release_year,
    y = percentage,
    fill = franchise_status
  )
) +
  geom_col(width = 0.9) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_percent()
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Original" = "#3478A8",
      "Franchise" = "#E59B46"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Release year",
    y = "Share of films",
    fill = "Film type"
  )

(p7 + p8 + p9) + plot_layout(ncol = 3)
```

Median budgets fluctuate rather than increasing steadily between 1990 and 2016. Median ROI also changes across years but generally remains above 1. Most films remain originals throughout the period, although the franchise share varies from year to year. These patterns are descriptive and do not by themselves explain changes in film profitability.

## Summary for the Head of Production

The dataset is dominated by original films, with relatively few franchises. Typical production budgets are well below the largest blockbuster budgets, while ROI varies considerably between films. This makes the median more useful than the mean for describing a typical project.

Production scale differs across genres: action and animation tend to need larger budgets, while horror and drama often operate at lower levels. ROI remains variable within every genre, so genre or budget alone should not be treated as a reliable predictor of financial success.

Finally, missing financial values are substantial: only **3,214 films** have both a valid budget and ROI. Comparisons should be viewed as exploratory, especially because box-office revenue is not the same as studio profit and ROI here does not deduct marketing or distribution costs.
